title: 22. Interview: SQL Databases
summary: Interview Q&A for SQL Databases — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 SQL Databases interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What are the four sub-languages of SQL, and why does the distinction matter operationally?
**Answer:** SQL is partitioned into DDL (Data Definition Language — `CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`), DML (Data Manipulation Language — `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `SELECT`), DCL (Data Control Language — `GRANT`, `REVOKE`), and TCL (Transaction Control Language — `BEGIN`, `COMMIT`, `ROLLBACK`, `SAVEPOINT`). The distinction matters because each category has different risk profiles and ownership. DDL changes alter the schema and can lock tables or break application code, so they are gated by migration tools (Flyway, Alembic, Liquibase) and code review. DML is the steady-state traffic emitted by application code; it is safe to run any time the schema is stable. DCL is owned by security/DBA teams and is audited for compliance (who can read PII?). TCL is the language of atomic business operations — placing an order, transferring money — and bugs in transaction boundaries cause the worst kind of production incident: silently inconsistent data.
**Visual:**
```
DDL  CREATE TABLE users (...)         <- migration tool, code review
DML  INSERT INTO users VALUES (...)   <- application code, every request
DCL  GRANT SELECT ON users TO app     <- DBA / security team
TCL  BEGIN; ...; COMMIT;              <- business logic, atomic units
```

### Q2. What is the relational model, and what problem did Codd's 1970 paper solve?
**Answer:** Codd's relational model represents data as relations (tables) of tuples (rows) with named attributes (columns), and lets users query the data declaratively without specifying access paths. Before 1970, the dominant databases were hierarchical (IBM IMS) and network (CODASYL) models, where queries required navigating physical pointers — programmers had to know the data's physical layout, and any structural change broke application code. The relational model's key insight was data independence: the logical schema (tables, foreign keys) is decoupled from the physical storage (files, indexes, pages), so the DBA can add an index or repartition a table without rewriting applications. SQL's declarative nature means the optimizer chooses the access path at runtime. This separation made relational databases the dominant data model for 50+ years and is the foundation of PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server, and SQLite.
**Visual:**
```
Pre-1970 (hierarchical):  GET customer>order>lineitem via pointer chase
                          (programmer knows physical layout)

Relational (1970):        SELECT c.name, o.total
                            FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id=o.cust_id
                          (optimizer chooses index/hash/scan)
```

### Q3. What is the difference between a primary key, a unique constraint, and a foreign key?
**Answer:** A **primary key** is a column (or composite of columns) that uniquely identifies each row and is `NOT NULL` by definition — there can be only one primary key per table. A **unique constraint** also enforces uniqueness but allows `NULL` values (multiple NULLs are permitted by the SQL standard, though some engines differ) and you can have many unique constraints per table. A **foreign key** is a column (or set) that references the primary key (or a unique column) of another table, enforcing referential integrity — you cannot insert an `order` with `user_id = 999` if no user 999 exists, and you cannot delete a user who has orders (unless `ON DELETE CASCADE` or `SET NULL` is configured). Foreign keys are the backbone of normalization: they make the relationships between tables explicit and enforceable by the database rather than by application code, preventing "orphan rows" that point to deleted parents.
**Visual:**
```
users(id PK, email UNIQUE, ...)         orders(id PK, user_id FK -> users.id)
+----+------------+                    +----+---------+
| id | email      |                    | id | user_id |
+----+------------+                    +----+---------+
|  1 | ada@x.com  |  <--- referenced - | 101|    1    |  ok
|  2 | alan@y.com |                    | 102|   999   |  REJECTED (no user 999)
+----+------------+                    +----+---------+
PK: not null, unique, one per table    FK: must reference existing PK in parent
UNIQUE: may be null, many per table
```

### Q4. When should you choose SQL over NoSQL, and what is the most common mistake teams make?
**Answer:** Choose SQL when the data is highly structured, relationships between entities matter (foreign keys, joins), and strong consistency is non-negotiable (financial transactions, inventory, user accounts, order placement). Choose NoSQL when the workload is key-value access at extreme scale (DynamoDB for session state, Cassandra for time-series), the data model is naturally hierarchical or schema-flexible (MongoDB for product catalogs with varying attributes), or write throughput exceeds what a single SQL primary can handle. The most common mistake is choosing NoSQL for "flexibility" early in a project, then discovering the application actually needs transactions and joins — at which point engineers emulate them in application code, badly, and the system develops consistency bugs that are extremely hard to debug. A sound default is to start with PostgreSQL and only move to NoSQL when you can articulate a specific scaling problem SQL cannot solve. "We might need to scale someday" is not a specific problem.
**Visual:**
```
SQL (PostgreSQL, MySQL)            NoSQL (DynamoDB, Cassandra, MongoDB)
- structured schema                - flexible / schemaless
- ACID transactions                - eventual consistency (usually)
- joins, foreign keys              - denormalized, key-value access
- scales vertically first         - scales horizontally by design
- default for money, orders, users - default for sessions, events, catalogs
```

### Q5. What is normalization, and when should you deliberately denormalize?
**Answer:** Normalization is the process of decomposing tables to eliminate redundancy and update anomalies, typically aiming for 3NF or BCNF. For example, instead of storing the customer's full address on every order row (which means an address change requires updating thousands of rows and risks inconsistency), you store `customer_id` on the order and join to the `customers` table when needed. Normalization saves storage, prevents anomalies, and keeps the schema flexible. Deliberate denormalization is appropriate when reads vastly outnumber writes, the denormalized data changes rarely, and the joined data is almost always read together — for example, copying `customer_name` onto the `order` row because every order-detail view shows the customer's name and customer names rarely change. The trade-off is faster reads at the cost of more careful writes (you must keep the copy in sync). Denormalization is also the standard pattern in analytics warehouses (star schemas), where query speed matters more than write simplicity.
**Visual:**
```
Normalized (3NF):
  orders(id, customer_id, total)  customers(id, name, address)
  -> JOIN to display name + address

Denormalized (for fast reads):
  orders(id, customer_id, customer_name, total)
  -> no JOIN needed; customer_name duplicated
  -> write must update orders.customer_name when customer changes name
```

### Q6. What is a schema migration, and why are they scary in production?
**Answer:** A schema migration is a controlled DDL change to a live database — adding a column, creating an index, changing a column type, or renaming a table. They are scary because they can lock the table (blocking all reads and writes), break application code that expects the old schema, or be irreversible without data loss. The standard playbook for safe migrations is: (1) make changes backward-compatible — add the new column as nullable, deploy application code that writes to both old and new, backfill the new column, then deploy code that reads only the new column, then drop the old column in a later deploy. (2) For adding indexes on large tables, use `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` (PostgreSQL) which builds the index without taking an exclusive lock. (3) For column type changes, add a new column, backfill, switch, then drop — never `ALTER COLUMN TYPE` directly on a billion-row table. (4) Always test migrations on a production-sized staging copy. Tools like Flyway, Alembic, and Liquibase version-control migrations so they apply in order and exactly once.
**Visual:**
```
Dangerous:    ALTER TABLE users ALTER COLUMN phone TYPE BIGINT;
              (locks table, rewrites every row, hours on a 1B-row table)

Safe pattern:
  1. ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN phone_new BIGINT;        (fast, nullable)
  2. deploy app that writes to BOTH phone and phone_new
  3. backfill: UPDATE users SET phone_new = phone::bigint  (batched)
  4. deploy app that reads only phone_new
  5. ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN phone;                  (later deploy)
  6. RENAME COLUMN phone_new TO phone;
```

### Q7. Why do SQL databases enforce the schema before writing, and what is the trade-off versus schemaless stores?
**Answer:** SQL databases enforce the schema (column types, `NOT NULL`, `CHECK`, `UNIQUE`, foreign keys) at write time, rejecting malformed rows at the database boundary. The benefit is that application code can rely on invariants being true for every row — you never have to write `if row.email is not None` defensively because the `NOT NULL` constraint guarantees it. This catches bugs early: a service that forgets to populate a required field fails loudly at insert time, not silently months later when a report shows NULLs. The trade-off is rigidity — schema changes require migrations, which are slow and risky in production. Schemaless stores (MongoDB, DynamoDB) accept any shape of document, which accelerates early development but shifts validation to application code. The consequence is that "schemaless" usually means "implicit schema enforced by application code," and inconsistencies accumulate when different services write slightly different shapes. Mature schemaless deployments end up reinventing schema validation in a JSON-Schema layer. The pragmatic choice is SQL when the data model is stable enough that the schema is a feature, not a friction.
**Visual:**
```
SQL:        DB rejects bad row at INSERT time
            INSERT INTO users(id, email) VALUES (1, NULL);
            -> ERROR: NOT NULL constraint failed: users.email

Schemaless: DB accepts anything; app must validate
            {"id":1}                  <- accepted, missing email
            {"id":1,"email":null}     <- accepted, null email
            {"id":"1","email":"x"}    <- accepted, wrong id type
            -> bugs surface later in reports
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. You're building Amazon's order service. Orders touch `users`, `orders`, `order_items`, `payments`, and `inventory`. Why is SQL the right choice, and how would you lay out the schema?
**Answer:** The order service needs multi-table atomicity: decrementing inventory, creating the order row, recording payment, and writing line items must all succeed or all fail — partial completion leaves the system in an inconsistent state (e.g., inventory decremented but no order row). SQL's ACID transactions across tables guarantee this atomicity in a single `BEGIN ... COMMIT`. The schema: `users(id, name, email, created_at)`; `orders(id, user_id FK, status, total_cents, created_at)`; `order_items(id, order_id FK, sku, qty, unit_price)`; `payments(id, order_id FK, provider, amount_cents, status)`; `inventory(sku PK, qty_on_hand, reserved)`. Foreign keys enforce referential integrity (no order without a user, no payment without an order). Money is stored as integer cents to avoid floating-point rounding. The `inventory.reserved` column supports a two-phase pattern: reserve stock on order placement, decrement `qty_on_hand` on shipment. For scale, partition `orders` by `created_at` (monthly) once you cross ~1B rows, and use a read replica for reporting queries so the transactional primary is not saturated by analytics.
**Visual:**
```
BEGIN;
  UPDATE inventory SET reserved = reserved + 2 WHERE sku='ABC';
  INSERT INTO orders(user_id, total_cents, status) VALUES (1, 4999, 'paid');
  INSERT INTO order_items(order_id, sku, qty, unit_price) VALUES (curr, 'ABC', 2, 2499);
  INSERT INTO payments(order_id, provider, amount_cents, status) VALUES (curr, 'visa', 4999, 'captured');
COMMIT;
   (all-or-nothing; if any step fails, ROLLBACK undoes the rest)
```

### Q2. Your team chose MongoDB for "schema flexibility" six months ago. Now you have 14 subtly different `user` document shapes in production, and reports are full of NULLs. How do you recover?
**Answer:** First, audit the actual shapes in production: write a script that groups documents by their key set and counts each group, so you can see which fields are missing where and why. Second, decide on a canonical schema — the union of fields every consumer actually needs, with explicit `nullable` rules. Third, deploy a schema-validation layer at the write path: MongoDB supports `$jsonSchema` validators (since 3.6), so configure `validator` on the collection to reject writes that don't match. Fourth, backfill the missing fields with sensible defaults or by joining against the source-of-truth service. Fifth, instrument application code to log a warning on any document that fails validation, so you catch the remaining inconsistent writers. The deeper lesson is "schemaless" usually means "implicit schema enforced by application code" — and when multiple services write the same collection, those implicit schemas drift. Long-term, consider whether MongoDB is even the right choice; a PostgreSQL table with JSONB columns gives you both schema enforcement and field-level flexibility, often a better fit for this kind of workload.
**Visual:**
```
Before: 14 shapes in production
  {name, email}                          (3.2M docs)
  {name, email, phone}                   (1.1M docs)
  {name, email, created_at}              (890K docs)
  {name}                                 (12K docs, legacy)
  ...

After: $jsonSchema validator
  required: ["name","email","created_at"]
  properties: { phone: { bsonType: ["string","null"] } }

Backfill: UPDATE users SET created_at = NOW() WHERE created_at IS NULL
```

### Q3. You're scaling a PostgreSQL-backed SaaS and hitting connection limits (max_connections = 100, app wants 5000). How do you solve it?
**Answer:** PostgreSQL's process-per-connection model means each idle connection still consumes memory (5–10 MB) and a process slot, so 5000 connections exhausts RAM and the postmaster's process table. The standard solution is a connection pooler like PgBouncer or pgcat in front of PostgreSQL, configured in transaction-pooling mode: clients connect to PgBouncer, which maintains a small pool (e.g., 50–100) of real backend connections to PostgreSQL and multiplexes client queries onto them. Transaction pooling reuses a backend connection per transaction rather than per client session, so 5000 idle clients share 100 backends with no contention. The trade-off is that transaction-pooling mode breaks session-level features (server-side prepared statements, `SET` commands, temporary tables, `LISTEN/NOTIFY`) — those features require session-pooling mode, which is less efficient. The other half of the solution is to reduce the number of connections the application opens: configure the ORM's connection pool (e.g., HikariCP for Java, SQLAlchemy pool for Python) to a sensible max (say 20 per instance), so 100 app instances = 2000 client connections to PgBouncer, multiplexed down to 100 PostgreSQL backends.
**Visual:**
```
5000 app instances \                              / 100 real PG backends
                   >  PgBouncer (transaction mode)  \
   (multiplexed)                                      / (5-10MB each)
                                                       |
                                                  PostgreSQL
```

### Q4. Your microservice writes to PostgreSQL. The DB team wants to enforce a CHECK constraint that breaks half your existing rows. How do you roll out the constraint safely?
**Answer:** Adding a `CHECK` constraint that existing rows violate will fail the `ALTER TABLE` and (in older PostgreSQL) may also take an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock that blocks reads and writes while it scans the table. The safe rollout is the "validate later" pattern: (1) add the constraint as `NOT VALID` — this is metadata-only, instant, does not scan the table, and does not block writes; new writes are checked immediately, but existing rows are not. (2) Run `ALTER TABLE ... VALIDATE CONSTRAINT ...` — this scans the table to verify existing rows satisfy the constraint, but it does so with a share-update lock, so writes are not blocked. (3) If validation fails, fix the offending rows with `UPDATE` statements, then re-validate. (4) If validation succeeds, the constraint is fully enforced. This pattern lets you ship the constraint in stages: deploy the `NOT VALID` constraint today, fix the bad rows over the next sprint, and validate next week. It is the database equivalent of feature-flagging a breaking change.
**Visual:**
```
Day 1:  ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT chk_total CHECK (total_cents >= 0) NOT VALID;
        (instant, no scan; new writes checked, old rows untouched)

Day 7:  UPDATE orders SET total_cents = 0 WHERE total_cents < 0;   (fix 3 bad rows)

Day 8:  ALTER TABLE orders VALIDATE CONSTRAINT chk_total;
        (scans table with share-update lock; passes; constraint fully enforced)
```

### Q5. Your analytics team runs ad-hoc `SELECT * FROM orders` queries against the production PostgreSQL primary and is slowing down checkout. What's the fix?
**Answer:** The fundamental issue is mixing OLTP (transactional, short, indexed) and OLAP (analytical, long, full-scan) workloads on the same database, which causes resource contention: the analytics query holds shared locks and saturates I/O, starving the checkout transaction. The first fix is to add a read replica (PostgreSQL streaming replication) and point analytics queries at it — replication is async, so the replica may lag a few seconds, but that's fine for analytics. The second fix is to set `statement_timeout` for the analytics role (e.g., 30 seconds) so a runaway `SELECT *` fails instead of running for an hour. The third fix is to add the indexes analytics actually needs (often a covering index on `(created_at, status, user_id)`) so common reports are index-only scans. The fourth fix, if analytics volume grows, is to move the data to a columnar warehouse (Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift) via CDC (Debezium → Kafka → warehouse), which is what Amazon, Netflix, and Uber all do at scale. Same data, different engine optimized for the workload.
**Visual:**
```
Before:  checkout queries <---> [primary] <---> analytics queries
         (contention; checkout latency spikes)

After:   checkout queries <---> [primary] --stream--> [read replica] <---> analytics
                                   (async, ~1s lag)        (statement_timeout=30s)

Mature:  primary --CDC/Debezium--> Kafka --> [columnar warehouse] <---> BI
         (checkout untouched; analytics runs on a separate engine)
```

### Q6. You're designing a multi-tenant SaaS. Should you use one database with a `tenant_id` column, a schema per tenant, or a database per tenant? What are the trade-offs?
**Answer:** The three models sit on a spectrum of isolation vs operational simplicity. **Shared database, shared schema (one `tenant_id` column)** is the cheapest: one schema to migrate, one connection pool, easy to scale to thousands of tenants. Every query must filter `WHERE tenant_id = ?`, and a missing filter leaks data across tenants — enforce this at the ORM or with row-level security (PostgreSQL RLS). Backup and restore are all-or-nothing (you can't restore just one tenant). **Schema-per-tenant** gives moderate isolation: tenants share the database process but have separate namespaces, so a missing `WHERE tenant_id` is structurally impossible. Migrations must run N times (once per schema). Connection pooling gets tricky because each schema may need its own pool. **Database-per-tenant** gives strong isolation (a noisy tenant can't crash others, backups are per-tenant, you can place a tenant's DB in a specific region for data residency), but operational cost is high — N databases to patch, monitor, back up. The right choice depends on tenant count, size variance, and compliance: small/many tenants → shared schema; large/few tenants with compliance needs → database-per-tenant.
**Visual:**
```
Shared schema (cheap, scales to many tenants):
  orders(id, tenant_id, ...)  every query: WHERE tenant_id=?

Schema-per-tenant (moderate isolation):
  tenant_a.orders(id, ...)    tenant_b.orders(id, ...)   (one DB, many schemas)
  -> missing WHERE impossible; migrations run N times

Database-per-tenant (strong isolation):
  db_tenant_a.orders          db_tenant_b.orders         (separate DBs)
  -> per-tenant backup/restore, patching, monitoring overhead
```

### Q7. Your startup is choosing between PostgreSQL and DynamoDB for the user-authentication service. Walk me through the decision.
**Answer:** User auth is a classic SQL workload: structured data (id, email, password_hash, created_at), strong consistency requirements (a freshly created user must be immediately visible at login), uniqueness constraints (email must be unique), and frequent joins (user → roles → permissions). PostgreSQL is the obvious default — the `UNIQUE` constraint on `email` is enforced by the database, transactions ensure a half-created user cannot exist, and foreign keys make the user-role relationship explicit. DynamoDB would work for the simple `GetUserByEmail` access pattern, but you would have to enforce email uniqueness in application code (DynamoDB has no native unique constraint on a non-key attribute), implement transactional user+role creation with DynamoDB Transactions (which are limited and slower), and accept eventual consistency on global secondary indexes. DynamoDB shines for extreme-scale key-value access (session storage, shopping carts) where you don't need joins or cross-row transactions. For auth, PostgreSQL is simpler, safer, and free; only switch to DynamoDB if auth traffic grows so large that a single PostgreSQL primary cannot keep up — which, for most companies, never happens, and even then Aurora Serverless or Citus would be a smoother scaling path.
**Visual:**
```
Auth workload:
  - structured data (id, email, password_hash, roles)
  - uniqueness on email (DB-enforced)
  - transactions (create user + roles atomically)
  - joins (user -> roles -> permissions)
  -> PostgreSQL by default

DynamoDB fits when:
  - billions of items, single-row key access
  - no joins, no cross-row transactions
  - schemaless or sparse attributes
  (sessions, carts, event logs -- NOT auth)
```
